notes.title: Nvidia fell while the market bounced
body: On Friday, Nvidia rose 2.78% as chip stocks recovered from Thursday’s rout. By Monday morning the broader market was bouncing again and Nvidia was falling. Same stock, different headline. On Sunday, Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation after reports that its CEO, Jensen Huang, had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. The board said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised. Independent directors and outside counsel will oversee the review. That’s what the company has put on the record so far.

Start with last week, because the timing matters. Stocks initially rallied after the midterms. On Thursday, the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5% and the SOXX semiconductor ETF fell 12.15%. Reporting pointed to concern that Democratic wins could make it harder or slower to build data centers. That’s a specific risk to the AI trade. If a project can’t get permitted or powered on schedule, the equipment it was meant to house may ship later. That was an investor concern, and it still takes an actual change in permits or orders to show up in the business.

Nvidia closed last week down 8.80%, compared with a 13.13% drop for SOXX over the same five sessions. By that measure Nvidia held up better than its sector. Monday was a different comparison. AP reported a rising broader market and weakness in Nvidia after the board’s announcement. The split makes the company news a more plausible part of Monday’s move than it would be on a day when every chip stock was falling. It still doesn’t tell me how much of the move to put on the investigation.

Here’s the business question. Before the weekend, I was watching whether the people buying AI systems could get the financing and power to install them. I’m still watching that. Now there’s a second question about whether the inquiry changes anything customers, employees, or regulators actually do. A board announcement doesn’t answer either question. I’d watch for a change in customer delivery schedules or company guidance before I start treating a governance headline as a shipment forecast.

There’s a number I care about more than the size of the first red candle. It’s the gap between growth on the income statement and cash coming in the door. An order booked for a cluster is one thing. A customer ready to take delivery and pay is another. If the market is right about slower construction, I’d expect to see it first in delivery schedules, working capital or the way management describes the next quarter.

Nvidia reports on Nov. 17. I’ll read the board’s next update for the scope of the inquiry and the earnings release for data-center demand and delivery timing. The quickest way to lose the plot here is to let one stock chart answer both questions. The board has its work. I’ll be in the footnotes.

performance.window: Five sessions through Nov. 6, 2026 · close to close

notes.flowRemark: Friday’s options activity predates the board statement. I’m watching whether demand for protection persists after the news.
